The Least chub Iotichthys phlegethontis is a small, endemic cyprinid inhabiting isolated spring systems of the Bonneville Basin in western North America. Field surveys indicate that the maximum total length attained by this species is approximately 6.4 centimeters [Li = approximately 6.4 centimeters], a modest size typical of spring-dwelling minnows adapted to nutrient-poor, thermally stable environments. Growth trajectories derived from mark-recapture studies reveal a protracted period of somatic development, with individuals reaching the total length at which puberty is initiated at roughly 2.5 centimeters [Lp = roughly 2.5 centimeters]. This size is achieved during the first growing season, with gonadal differentiation commencing shortly thereafter in concert with rising spring temperatures. The species occupies a narrow thermal niche, and most reproductive and metabolic processes are tied to the relatively cool, stable water temperatures of its desert spring habitats, typically recorded near 13 °C [T = 13 °C] throughout the year.

Laboratory observations conducted at a stable water temperature of 13 °C [T = 13 °C] have provided detailed estimates of the species' reproductive output. Although direct fecundity data for Least chub remain limited, comparative studies on the morphologically similar Lepidomeda aliciae suggest that at a standard length of 92 millimeters and a total length of 108 millimeters, females deposit approximately 7.4 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 7.4 eggs per spawning event], and typically spawn once per year [F_R_i = spawn once per year]. This modest output, yielding about 7.4 eggs per individual per year, is consistent with an iteroparous life history strategy in which small-bodied, spring-adapted cyprinids allocate resources continuously across an extended breeding season rather than investing in a single, large batch of gametes.

Neonatal and early life history traits have been inferred from both direct observation and allometric relationships developed for related cyprinids. The newly hatched yolk-sac larva emerges at an extremely low wet weight of approximately 0.00052 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.00052 grams], reflecting the tiny egg size characteristic of this genus, a trait that imposes constraints on larval survival in oligotrophic spring habitats. At the completion of the larval period, following yolk-sac resorption and the onset of exogenous feeding, body mass increases substantially. Allometric equations calibrated for Western North American cyprinids predict a wet weight at the species' ultimate total length of around 2.61 grams [Wwi = around 2.61 grams], which serves as a benchmark for the maximum body mass achievable by a fully grown adult under optimal foraging conditions. This mass represents a considerable developmental investment from the minute hatchling stage.

Reproductive maturation is accompanied by a distinct shift in body mass, as energetic reserves are increasingly directed toward gonadal development. At the onset of puberty, which corresponds to a total length of approximately 2.5 centimeters, individual wet weight is estimated at approximately 0.147 grams [Wwp = approximately 0.147 grams], a value derived from length-mass regressions that account for the slender body morphology of this cyprinid. This weight threshold marks the transition from the juvenile growth phase to a reproductively capable adult state. Population surveys indicate that individuals achieving this size generally spawn during their second calendar year, with first reproduction typically occurring between April and July when water temperatures approach the species' preferred thermal regime.

Longevity in Least chub has been assessed through both otolith-based age estimation and long-term monitoring of marked individuals in stable spring environments. Maximum lifespan is estimated at approximately 7 years [am = approximately 7 years] under the cool, consistent thermal conditions typical of the species' native aquifer-fed habitats, where water temperature remains near 13 °C [T = 13 °C] year-round. This longevity allows individuals to spread reproductive effort over multiple seasons, reducing year-class variability in fluctuating environments. Age-structured population models suggest that this longevity allows multiple reproductive bouts across several seasons, buffering the population against occasional recruitment failures during drought years.
